newsitem.title: USA: Lawmakers ask Reno to review Teamsters election.
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers ask Reno to review Teamsters election.

text.p: Leaders of the House Judiciary Committee on Friday asked Attorney General Janet Reno to look into how the Teamsters Union election was handled by a court-appointed overseer.

In a letter to Reno, committee Chairman Henry Hyde, Republican of Illinois, and ranking minority member John Conyers, a Michigan Democrat, relayed complaints about the election process which were called to their attention by the apparent loser of the race, James Hoffa.
"We would appreciate your looking into these claims and a determination as to their merits," the lawmakers said.

Hoffa, 55, son of the late Jimmy Hoffa who ran the union in the 1950s and 1960s, has already asked Reno to impound the ballots and launch an FBI investigation into "serious irregularities" in the election.

He has complained of a discrepancy of at least 25,000 mail-in ballots and has formally protested other alleged ballot-counting irregularities in the process overseen by court-appointed Election Officer Barbara Zack Quindel.

Incomplete tallies show Teamsters Union President Ron Carey leading Hoffa. But Quindel has not declared a winner because Carey's margin over Hoffa was smaller than the number of so-called challenged ballots that are still being processed.
Carey, 60, who won the union's presidency as a reform candidate in 1991, has declared that he won re-election.

In the election, the second one held under the terms of a 1989 settlement of a federal anti-racketeering suit, ballots were mailed to some 1.4 million union members in early November. Ballot-counting began on Dec. 10 at a rented facility outside Washington.

Quindel has accounted for 485,605 mail-in ballots returned. But earlier, she reported that the U.S. Postal Service had billed her office for 511,268 ballots, more than 25,000 more than the number of ballots for which she is able to account.
Quindel's spokesman, Jeff O'Mara, said the Postal Service estimate was based on weight. He had no comment on the lawmakers' request for a Justice Department probe of the election.
Carey spokeswoman Renee Asher characterized the lawmakers' request for a Justice Department investigation as a "constituent service" by them for Hoffa.
"We think the election has been fair," she said. "The Teamsters have spoken. The election is over."

After processing nearly half of the 41,002 challenged ballots that were set aside for eligibility checks, Quindel reported on Thursday that Carey was still leading Hoffa by 230,142 to 215,034, with 20,529 challenged ballots still unprocessed and 14,474 others declared ineligible.
